About this manual

Thank you for choosing the Luchs B, a full-size off-road chassis for autonomous and remotely operated vehicles.

This manual explains how to operate the chassis safely and how to control it from your own computer. Please read it before you start, and keep it for future reference.

Who this manual is for

  • Autonomy and robotics engineers who integrate sensors, compute and software on the Luchs B and need the interface, the control modes and the safety behaviour in detail.
  • Operators who drive the vehicle by remote control, charge it and carry out daily checks.
  • Service engineers who commission, maintain and troubleshoot the chassis.

Software versions

This manual describes chassis firmware that implements the Luchs Chassis Interface (LCI) v1.0. This firmware is in development. Units shipped before it is released use the VCU interface V2.6, described in section 5.3. The ROS software (section 5.4) supports both.

CHAPTER 1Safety

Read before use

The Luchs B weighs about 230 kg and can reach 40 km/h. A vehicle of this size can cause serious injury. Read and understand all safety information in this manual before operating it.

Prohibited

Environment

  • Do not operate the chassis on public roads.
  • Do not charge the chassis in rain or snow, or anywhere the charging inlet may come into contact with water.
  • Do not operate the chassis in the presence of flammable or explosive gases.
  • Do not operate or store the chassis outside its operating temperature range of −20 °C to +55 °C.
  • Do not drive through water deeper than 300 mm.

Operation

  • Do not allow children, untrained persons, or anyone who is tired or under the influence of alcohol or medication to operate the chassis.
  • Do not ride on the chassis or let anyone ride on it.
  • Do not stand in front of or behind the chassis while it is powered, and keep a clear zone of at least 5 m around it while it moves.
  • Do not exceed the maximum payload of 200 kg, or the working payload of 80 kg for continuous operation.
  • Do not disassemble or service the chassis, or touch moving or hot parts (wheels, motors, brakes, power electronics), while it is switched on.

Charging

  • Use only the charging equipment approved for the chassis. An unsuitable power supply can cause fire.
  • Charge only at ambient temperatures between 0 °C and 55 °C.
  • If the battery overheats, smokes or smells unusual, stop charging immediately and move away.

Mandatory

Before each use

  • Walk once around the vehicle. Check the tyres, the bumpers, the deck load and its fixings, and that nothing is caught in the wheels.
  • Check that the emergency stop button and both bumpers stop the vehicle (section 4.5), and that the transmitter battery is charged.
  • When testing your own software, keep the transmitter in hand and a safety operator ready to stop the vehicle.

Charging and maintenance

  • Charge in a dry, well-ventilated place, away from flammable materials.
  • Use only original spare parts. If the chassis will not be used for a long time, keep the battery at 50–70 % and charge it regularly.
  • If any fault occurs, switch the chassis off and contact support. Do not attempt to repair high-voltage parts yourself.

In an emergency

  1. Press the emergency stop on the side panel, or flip switch A on the transmitter.
  2. Switch the chassis off.
  3. Follow your emergency plan, move people to safety and deal with the situation.

CHAPTER 2Product overview

2.1 Introduction

The Luchs B is a 4×4 off-road chassis designed to carry an autonomy stack. Four in-wheel motors, two electric power-steering units, an electro-hydraulic brake and an electric parking brake are all controlled by the chassis controller. Your computer sends motion commands over one CAN interface; the chassis executes them, protects itself and reports its state.

The Luchs B speaks the Luchs Chassis Interface (LCI). Its core frames use the same identifiers and layouts as the protocol of the smaller Luchs A, and one ROS software package drives both chassis: software written for one runs on the other with a change of vehicle parameters.

2.2 Key features

  • Off-road capable. 300 mm class ground clearance, independent suspension, 22-inch tyres, 4WD with 330 N·m peak torque per wheel.
  • Steering on both axles. Front Ackermann for stable high-speed driving, dual Ackermann for tight turns, selected by command.
  • Built to be driven by a computer. Motion-level commands, odometry-grade feedback, live limits, a host heartbeat and a documented DBC.
  • Layered safety. Emergency stops on the vehicle, the bumpers, the transmitter and the host interface; a parking brake that holds a full load on a 20° slope.

Desert mode (range extender)

Desert mode is the ultimate-endurance configuration: two battery packs of about 5 kWh each and a 1.5 kW range extender, all inside the frame, below the deck. The range extender charges the batteries while you drive and extends the range to up to 300 km. In photos and films of test vehicles you may see the range extender bolted to the deck; that is a test position for easy access.

The charging inlet shown is the type fitted to current units (250 V, 32 A); export units may use a different inlet.

The chassis is supplied with a 2.4 GHz handheld transmitter and a matching receiver fitted to the vehicle.

CHAPTER 3Quick start

Follow these steps to start your Luchs B safely. Before you begin, make sure you have read and understood Chapter 1.

3.1 Daily check

  1. Walk around the vehicle. Check the area is clear, the tyres are inflated and undamaged, and any load on the deck is secured.
  2. Check the emergency stop. Make sure the emergency stop button is released (turn it clockwise to release).
  3. Check the transmitter. Make sure it has battery and that switch A (emergency stop) is up and switch G (gear) is in neutral.

3.2 Power on and drive by remote control

  1. Switch on the chassis. Press the start button on the side panel. The battery display shows voltage, state of charge and current.
  2. Switch on the transmitter. Push its power switch up; the screen lights up.
  3. Select remote control. Set switch C up.
  4. Enable. Set switch F down.
  5. Set a speed limit. Turn knob VRC up from zero. Start low.
  6. Select a gear. Switch G to centre for forward, or down for reverse.
  7. Drive. Push the right stick up to drive and pull it down to brake. Steer with the left stick.

3.3 Power off

  1. Stop the vehicle and set switch G to neutral. The parking brake applies automatically when no control source is active.
  2. Switch off the chassis with the start button. The battery display goes dark.
  3. Switch off the transmitter.

3.4 Charging

  1. Switch off the chassis. The vehicle must be off while charging.
  2. Connect. Open the cover of the charging inlet on the side panel and plug in the charging connector firmly.
  3. Charge. The charge indicator shows progress. A full charge takes about 3 hours.
  4. Finish. Unplug the connector and close the inlet cover.

3.5 Connecting your computer

  1. Mount and wire your equipment on the deck. Connect your computer's CAN interface to the customer CAN port, and power your equipment from the payload power port (section 4.7).
  2. Configure CAN. 1 Mbit/s, standard 11-bit identifiers.
  3. Start the heartbeat. Send LCI_HostHeartbeat (0x5A5) every 20 ms. Without it the chassis will not move under host control (section 5.2.2).
  4. Hand over control. With the transmitter on and enabled, set switch C down. The chassis now follows your commands.
  5. Send commands. Start with low speeds. The ROS software (section 5.4) is the quickest way to get going: it sends the heartbeat for you.
Keep a way to stop

While your software is under development, keep the transmitter in hand. Flipping switch C up takes control back immediately; switch A stops the vehicle.

CHAPTER 4Functions in detail

4.1 Power-on self-test

At switch-on the chassis controller checks the battery management system, the four motor controllers, both steering units, the brake and the parking brake before it allows the vehicle to move. Faults are shown on the interface (section 5.4) and the vehicle stays parked.

4.2 Controls on the chassis

Table 4-1 · Side control panel (Figure 2-2)
No.ItemFunction
1Battery displayBattery voltage, state of charge and current. Lit while the chassis is on.
2Start buttonSwitches the chassis on and off.
3Emergency stopStops the vehicle (section 4.5). Turn clockwise to release.
4Charge indicatorShows charging progress.
5Service / CAN portWeatherproof 5-pin connector with the CAN bus (section 4.7).
6Payload power port24 V output for your equipment (section 4.7).
7Payload power switchSwitches the 24 V payload output on and off.
8Charging inletAC charging connection, with a weatherproof cover.

4.3 Remote control

The transmitter controls the vehicle only when all four conditions are met: the receiver has a valid signal, the transmitter is online, switch C is set to remote control, and switch F is set to enable.

Table 4-2 · Driving with the transmitter
ControlBehaviour
Right stick upDrive. Speed rises with stick travel up to the limit set with knob VRC. The vehicle only drives with a gear selected, a speed limit above zero, no brake demand, no emergency stop and no motor or battery fault.
Right stick downBrake, proportional to stick travel, up to full brake pressure (6 MPa).
Left stickSteering, proportional to stick travel. Steering speed falls as road speed rises: about 520 °/s at standstill down to about 130 °/s at top speed.
Both sticksA dead band of ±5 % around centre is ignored.
Knob VRCSets the top speed for remote control. Forward 0–30 km/h, reverse limited to 10 km/h in current firmware.

4.4 Control modes

The chassis always knows who is in control, and it, not the host computer, decides which source it accepts.

Table 4-3 · Control modes
ModeHow to enterAcceptsPurpose
Remote controlTransmitter online, switch F enable, switch C upTransmitterManual driving, moving the vehicle, supervising tests.
AutomaticTransmitter online, switch F enable, switch C down, host heartbeat presentHost computerYour autonomy software drives the vehicle over LCI.
MaintenancePlannedNeitherPlanned: motion locked out; used to clear faults and recover after an emergency stop without switching off.
No controlNo valid sourceNeitherIf moving, the vehicle brakes for 5 s to a stop and applies the parking brake; if stationary, it parks immediately.
Remote control always wins

The transmitter link is independent of the host interface. Setting switch C up, or switch A down, takes effect regardless of what the host computer is sending.

4.5 Safety functions

4.5.1 Emergency stop

Any of the following triggers an emergency stop:

  • the emergency stop button on the side panel,
  • the front or rear bumper strip,
  • switch A on the transmitter,
  • an emergency stop request from the host computer (LCI_HostHeartbeat, EStopRequest),
  • an external hard-wired stop loop on the payload connector (planned).

On an emergency stop the vehicle brakes at full pressure for 5 seconds and then applies the parking brake. The chassis reports which source triggered the stop (LCI_ChassisState, EStopSource).

Table 4-4 · Recovering from an emergency stop
FirmwareRecovery
CurrentRemove the cause, release the button, then switch the chassis off and on again.
Planned (LCI)Remove the cause, release the button, switch to maintenance mode, then back. No power cycle.

4.5.2 Bumpers

After a front-bumper contact the vehicle brakes for 5 seconds and can then only reverse. After a rear-bumper contact it brakes for 5 seconds and can then only drive forward.

4.5.3 Host heartbeat

In automatic mode the chassis expects LCI_HostHeartbeat every 20 ms. If it is missing for 200 ms, or its counter stops changing, the chassis brings the vehicle to a controlled stop, applies the parking brake and reports a heartbeat timeout. Available with the LCI firmware.

4.5.4 Live limits

The chassis limits speed and steering for slope, roll, temperature, battery state and faults. Commands above a limit are executed at the limit, not rejected, and the chassis reports the current limits and whether a command was clipped (LCI_LimitsFb). Available with the LCI firmware.

4.5.5 Parking brake

The electric parking brake applies automatically when the vehicle stops without a control source and after an emergency stop. It holds a fully loaded vehicle on a 20° slope for at least 5 minutes.

5.2 CAN protocol (LCI)

LCI is the CAN interface of the Luchs family; its core frames use the same identifiers and layouts as the Luchs A protocol.

Preliminary

LCI v1.0 is a draft and the Luchs B firmware that implements it is in development. Message IDs and layouts may still change.

StandardCAN 2.0B, standard 11-bit identifiers, 8-byte payload
Bit rate1 Mbit/s, on a dedicated customer CAN channel
Byte orderBig-endian (Motorola): the high byte of a multi-byte signal is sent first. Signed values in two's complement.
Physical valueRaw value × factor + offset
Command levelMotion level only: target speed with a yaw rate, or with front and rear road-wheel angles, plus an optional acceleration limit. The chassis closes the speed, steering and brake loops. There are no throttle, brake-pressure or steering-motor commands.
TimingHost commands every 20 ms (any period up to 50 ms is accepted). Feedback every 20 ms; IMU every 10 ms.
Who is in chargeThe host states intent; the chassis is the final authority on modes, limits and stopping.

5.2.1 Reference frame and motion models

All motion values refer to the rear-axle centre on the ground, with X forward, Y left and Z up (ROS REP 103). Yaw is positive anticlockwise seen from above.

Table 5-2 · Motion models on Luchs B (KinematicModel)
ValueModelSteering from yaw rate
0x02Front Ackermannδf = atan(L · ωz / vx), rear axle straight
0x04Dual Ackermannδf = −δr = atan(L · ωz / (2 vx)). The rear-axle centre moves sideways: vy = −ωz · L / 2, reported in ActualVy.
0x01Skid-steerNot offered on Luchs B

L is the wheelbase, 1.430 m. Set SteerSource in LCI_SteerCmd to 1 to command road-wheel angles directly instead of a yaw rate; this also works at standstill.

5.2.2 Heartbeat and timeouts

  • Send LCI_HostHeartbeat (0x5A5) every 20 ms, increment AliveCounter by 1 in every frame (255 wraps to 0), and set Checksum to the low byte of the sum of bytes 0–6, XOR 0xFF.
  • If the heartbeat is missing for 200 ms, or AliveCounter stops changing, the chassis stops under control, parks and sets EStopSource bit 7.
  • EStopRequest is always executed as an emergency stop. Use ParkRequest when you want the chassis to stop under control.

Table 5-4 · LCI message definitions
PositionSignalTypeScalingValues and notes

bytes 2–3TargetVyint160.001 m/sLateral speed, +left. 4WS only; others send 0

byte 7ControlModeuint810x00 = autonomous (only value)

Gear and axle steering angles for Ackermann-type chassis.
byte 0Gearuint810=disabled 1=P 2=R 3=N 4=D

bytes 3–4RearSteerAngleint160.001 radRoad-wheel angle, rear axle, +left (dual Ackermann / AWS)

byte 0TurnIndicatoruint810=off 1=left 2=right 3=hazard (3 new in r3)

0x5A4  LCI_HostTime  ·  Host → Chassis  ·  1 s
Host wall-clock time so chassis logs and fault records can be matched to host logs.
bytes 0–7HostTimeMsuint641 msMilliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC

byte 0AliveCounteruint81Increments by 1 every frame, wraps 255→0

5.3 VCU interface V2.6

Luchs B units shipped before the LCI firmware use the upper-computer interface of the vehicle control unit. It works at pedal level: your software sets the accelerator and brake, the road-wheel angle and a speed cap, and the chassis reports its speed in whole km/h. It is suited to bring-up, teleoperation and data recording; for autonomy use LCI. The ROS software supports it with protocol:=legacy_b and closes the speed loop for you.

Table 5-5 · VCU interface V2.6
MessageDirection · cycleContent
0x701 UpperCmdHost → Chassis · 10 msAccelerator and brake (%), road-wheel angle (±42°), speed cap (km/h), steering rate, upper-computer control, headlight, emergency stop, park, gear (N / D / R), heartbeat
0x703 VCU2UpperChassis → Host · 10 msState of charge, battery temperature and voltage, fault level, gear, mode, speed (km/h), heartbeat

Byte order little-endian (Intel). Before the first drive, check the bit rate (500 kbit/s) and the sign of the steering angle on your vehicle; the ROS software sets both by parameter. Full definitions: Luchs_B_CAN_Protocol_VCU_V2.6.xlsx and Luchs_B_CAN_VCU_V2.6.dbc.

5.4 ROS software

The ROS software for the Luchs family is supplied as luchs_ros2 (version 1.1, ROS 2 Humble and Jazzy) and luchs_ros1 (version 1.1, ROS 1 Noetic). Both are built on the same ROS-independent C++ SDK and drive Luchs B and Luchs A from one code base, with the same topics, frames and services. Publish a velocity on cmd_vel; the driver sends the LCI commands and the heartbeat every 20 ms, applies the live limits the chassis reports (keeping the path curvature), and stops when commands or feedback stop. If the driver process stops, the heartbeat stops and the chassis parks by itself within 200 ms.

Table 5-6 · Main topics and services of the driver
DirectionTopic / serviceTypeContent
Subscribedcmd_velgeometry_msgs/TwistVelocity: forward and yaw rate (dual or front Ackermann)
Publishedodomnav_msgs/OdometryOdometry at base_link and the odom → base_footprint transform
Publishedimu/data_rawsensor_msgs/ImuChassis IMU (LCI 0x5BE / 0x5B1)
Published~/state · ~/safetyluchs_msgs/…Control mode, e-stop source, live limits, EPB / EPS / brake, temperatures, model and firmware
Publishedjoint_states · battery_state · /diagnosticssensor_msgs/… · diagnostic_msgs/…Steering and wheel joints, battery, link and fault status
Service~/estop · ~/parkstd_srvs/SetBoolEmergency-stop and park requests in the heartbeat
Service~/set_speed_limit · ~/set_payload_powerluchs_msgs/…Host speed cap; switched payload outputs

Quick start (ROS 2): bring the CAN interface up at 1 Mbit/s (setup_can.sh can0), set switch C down, then ros2 launch luchs_bringup luchs_b.launch.py; units with the VCU interface: add protocol:=legacy_b. ROS 1: roslaunch luchs_bringup luchs_b.launch. Without a vehicle, add dry_run:=true to run against the built-in simulator, which follows LCI including the heartbeat timeout. The README and the docs folder in each package cover installation, wiring, parameters and troubleshooting.

The software has been validated against the built-in simulator.

5.5 Autonomy by TAR (option)

The Luchs family is built for autonomy. TerraAgent Robotics (TAR) supplies it as an option: sensor kit, compute, positioning, perception, planning, vehicle control and the control station, integrated on the Luchs B and delivered as one system. TAR software drives the chassis through the interfaces and the ROS driver described in this chapter, so sections 5.1 to 5.4 apply to a vehicle with the TAR kit as well. Figure 5-1 shows building blocks that already run on real vehicles and real data.

  • Positioning degrades safely: RTK, then visual-inertial coasting at reduced speed, then a timed safe stop; LiDAR map localisation is the second source when satellites drop out.
  • Perception is camera-first, with LiDAR and radar added per application: 3D detection, a drivable-ground map and a live elevation map for holes and steps.
  • Planning runs in three layers (route, behaviour, trajectory) and hands its commands to the chassis through the ROS driver.

The functions, the sensor kit and the delivery for your site are agreed with TAR. Contact details are in section 6.3.

CHAPTER 6Maintenance and support

6.1 Routine care

  • Check tyre condition before each use.
  • Keep the battery between 50 % and 70 % for storage longer than a month, and charge it at least every 3 months.
  • Clean mud and sand from the wheels, suspension and bumper strips after off-road use. Do not use a high-pressure washer on connectors or controllers.
  • Battery swap takes under 3 minutes with the correct tools.

6.2 Warranty

Chassis: 12 months or 2000 km off-road / 4000 km paved, whichever comes first. Repairs: 90 days on the same issue. Excludes normal wear, consumables and damage from misuse, accident or unauthorised modification.

APPENDIX CTerms and abbreviations

2WD / 4WDTwo- or four-wheel drive.
Ackermann steeringCar-style steering in which the inner wheel turns more sharply than the outer one, so both follow the same arc.
BMSBattery Management System.
CANController Area Network: a robust two-wire bus used in vehicles and machines.
DBCA standard file format describing CAN messages and signals.
Dual AckermannBoth axles steer, in opposite directions, for a tighter turn.
EPBElectric Parking Brake.
EPSElectric Power Steering.
HeartbeatA message the host sends at a fixed rate so the chassis knows it is alive.
IMUInertial Measurement Unit: measures rotation rates and accelerations.
LCILuchs Chassis Interface.
OdometryAn estimate of the vehicle's motion from wheel speeds and steering angles.
REP 103The ROS convention for units and coordinate frames.
ROS 2Robot Operating System 2.
Yaw rateHow fast the vehicle turns about its vertical axis.
